I, I, I doubt not but sheele turne: but t'will bee like a Buzzard Hawke that turnes her tayle to her game. Is not that alwayes going? O thou hast wit I see I am in loue boy, I am, I am. With a verie Wagtaile an'arrant woman, a verie Peace whose pride is maintaind by her taile. And I will rather die a shamefull death, then liue a hatefull life, which I must do vnlesse I find a meanes that may deserue your loue. Durst I? I vowe, euen by my soules eternitie, I durst. What is't deare Ladie? although it be the death of man, if it be pleasing vnto you Ile doo't. But what are they Ladies? I haue a Countrey-man in towne an Apothecarie, one Signeur Aluino, a fellow that is well stor'd, and will sell me of the best. Still tonguelesse night put off thy sable robe, Thou needs not mourne, my villanies were done By day, thou hadst no hand in them, O I am great, as is a woman that is neare her time: And life's the burthen that I beare. But t'is a bastard for that I am asha'md on't. The Law I hope is a skilfull midwife, and will soone deli uer me; grim Iustice doe thy worst, Thy crueltie shall prooue a curtesie, And baile me out of prison. Lie there thou selfe-consuming Taper, true patern of my life, I haue consumde my selfe for others, as thou hast done for mee, and nowe shee has extinguisht my life as I this light. O how obedient was my bountie, still To her commaund? my liberalitie Did fatten mischiefe, and hath made her prowde: O that too much of any thing shuld be so ill in euery thing The Suns all seeng eye, with too much vntemperate heate makes wither what it made to flourish. The earth being mother to all wholsome hearbes, With too much fatnesse oft produceth weedes. A sute of cloath doth keepe the bodie warme, When richer garments makes the wearer proude. O, the meanes the sweetest Musicke; Contentment reuels when that string is toucht; But O, the time will come she will repent My death: for when she lookes on vices face Vnmaske like mine; she will detest and loath it. For this is truth and euermore hath bin, None can forsake before he knowes his sinne.
And let Tobacco be your perfumes. Sure I was a foole. Indeed I was, indeed I was. Faith Ladie these Gentlewomen haue not long v sed my companie, yet you see how Tobacco hath alreadie refined their spirits. Why, what ayles my nose? Why doy' play so about my nose? Deare Ladie, now by this day I loue you. Faith Ladie I must enquire your name. O, I know tit well inough. Come, come, Ladie can you loue? And can you loue me? Euerie foole can say, I, and no, Doy' thinke I want wit? Good Ladie, haue a better regarde of mee, doe but thinke me made of the same mettall other men are. Why, what mettall doe you thinke me? Deare Ladie, now by this day I loue you. Sir, would you make my Ladie and me friends? Ladie, I must confesse I haue offred you an emptie pipe, which me thinks hath smal reason to be take ̄ in snuff. I with all my heart. Nost willingly. Most willingly. Neuer. Neuer? I'me in a faire case now. Well, ile keepe my oath, farewell Gentlemen. O Fleire, how doost Fleire? How doe thy two Ladies liue Fleire? Thou their leader! why doe they meane to goe to the warres? Dost heare Fleir? woot prefer me to their seruice? I will tell her she is so wise, that neither age nor time could cousen her of beautie. I will tell her that I loue her most for the whitenes of her skin. I will praise the smalnes of her fingars. I am affraide that being olde shee has a drye hand. As I am truely generous, shee's modest. Faire Mistris, you are so wise, that neither time nor age could euer cousen you of beautie, and I sweare euen by the Alpes high heauen-touching tops, the trauelers narrowe passage, and by the towring head of high mount Chiego, the Sea-ma ̄ s southward marke: by these the witnesses vnto my trauell, I doe vow that you are passing fayre. O be not angry, for I protest I cannot but commend the whitenes of your skin. Now on my conscience Mistresse, my loue is honest, and I desire marriage. At our next meeting we wil set down a day for the effecting of it. Faith ill newes, the two Florentine Ladies, with Maister Sparke and Maister Ruffell were all poysoned yest erday at a feast by your Lord Piso and the Knight, but the Ladies haue recouered their health, but Sparke and Ruffell are dead, and their burial is committed to Fleire: your Lord & the Knight are committed to prison, & shal to morrow be arraign'd for the murther, and tride by the Ciuill-lawe, because your Lord is a stranger, and claimes to be tride by the law of nations.
speeches.Nan,: Lord Gentlemen how your wits Caper! me thinkes twould become you well at first entrance, your discretions came in with a sober measure. Neuer we sir: As the clapper of a Mill, my Lord. If a hundred men in a company, mee't doth not the worthiest man amongst them, first take his place, and sit downe? O Signior Petoune, what newes? Well Signior ile commit you to God.
Ladies we are come to make a Gentleman of your ac quaintance heere. But since, it hath imbellisht his good parts, perfec ted his ill partes, and made his secrete actions correspon dent to his outward wisdome, as you may well perceiue. Now Ladie, what drugs of wit has this Apothecarie of Tobacco sold you? By the diuine smoke of Tobacco signeur, you haue sham'd vs all. Why, proue signeur, you can but trie, weele al speake for you. Why Signior, I hope you wonnot swagger? Nothing else? Shall I preferre thee? Nai't shall be to a couple of Gentlewomen of thine owne Countrie. I. Why thou shalt serue but one, yet take thy choice of both. Whats thy name? Faire Ladies youle excuse vs. Saue ye Gentles. Faith I haue been with two Gentlewomen, in whose companie thou first sawst vs, and there the Knight, Sir Iohn Haue-little is so in loue with the younger, as a knowes not whether a should reioyce, shee had so much beautie: or la ment, because he is like to inioy none on't. We are euen readie for your two Ladies Signeur; Madam, the loue that I may giue you, fully doe in ioy, but I haue sworne with other loue then as a Brother doth a sister neuer to loue any. No, Ladies our occasions cals vs hence, and I am sorrye we must leaue you. But come Signior, how will you woe her? And what fees hast thou out of their trade? Faith I, poore Signior, I see the Springle of her beau tie hath alreadie caught the Woodcocke of his affections. Me thought t'was long, as long as a suit hangs here in the Law ere it be ended. Faith I saw the foure sonnes of Aymon, and they were Porters euer since there was a companie made of am. Yes, I sawe a Citizen damn'd for refusing a de sperate debt, because t'was tendred him on a Sabboth. Alas man they seldom conuerse with a good Angell scarce once in a whole Michaelmasse Tearme, and if a come a stayes not long with am to feede these soules, for they are faine to sende am away strayght to pay for the feeding of their Horses, there was a Chamber maide damb'd for keeping her virginitie till shee was mar ryed, and there were many Soldiers damb'd for saying their prayers when they were drunke.
speeches.Spar,: His name is Sig. Petoune a Traueller and a great To baconist.
speeches.Pet:: Faith Ladyes I take it now and then fasting for the purification of my wit. Faith Ladies if you vsde but mornings when ye rise, the diuine smoke of this Celestiall herbe, it will more puri fie, clense and mundifie your complexions, by ten partes then your dissolued Mercury, your iuice of Lemmons, your distilled snailes, your gourd waters, your oyle of rar tar, or a thousand such toyes. Indeed I was a very silly fellow. Indeed I was an Idiot, a verie Idiot. Will you teach me? Ile come to you to schoole. Prethe peace: deare Ladie, please you take a pipe of Tobacco? Sweare not good sir, sweare not, prophane not the Indian plant. But wil she forgiue me thinke you if I ask eher mer cie on my knees? Neuer. Neuer Well, some shall smoke for this. Hang her, hang her, shees a very crickee, shee hath written for me three or foure times, but ile see her damn'd ere ile come to her, woot take anie Tobacco Fleire? Thou art a good Courtier Fleire, tha'st got a sute alreadie. Prithe what are they? Why? I heere say they liue gallantly. And what art thou? a Sumner? Because thou art one of the; harke in thine eare. I thinke Fleir thy Ladies are not wee rich. I pray sir what may she be worth? A Foule Lady? what bird might that be? Gods mee; shee's angrie, what shall I doe now Signior? I pray you Ladie knowe mee by the title of some kindenes. I my Heroique spirits, ile followe yee.
speeches.Sus:: Purification? why has your wit layne in child-bed sir? I pra'y doe sir, yond Gentlewoman knowes it. No. And I alwayes answere euerie foole so. If others were of the same mettall you are, and all mine, I should quickelie sell them to the Bel-ma kers. Copper sir, copper, for I take your bodie to be of the same mettall your nose is. Signeur, you see these Gentlewomen haue not long vsed your companie; yet you see how Tobacco hath al readie refined their spirits: Come maister First you shall neuer while you liue offer Ladie or Gentlewoman an emptie pipe.
Sure Ladies I must needes say th' instinct of this herb hath wrought in this Gentleman such a diuine influence of good words, excelle ̄ t discourse, admirable inuention, inco ̄ parable wit: why I tel yee, when he talkes, wisdom stands a mile off and dares not come neere him, for feare a should shame her: but before a did vse this Tobacco, a was the ar rantst Woodcock that euer I saw. Hayda, this is like a Lawyers studdie in the latter end of a Terme, one's no sooner thrung'd out, but another's thrust in, y'are welcome sir.
Nay you were an arrant asse. No, but I meane the Cittizens must cuckold the courtiers Yea, how Fleire how? One that procures meanes for procreation, vul garly cald a Pander. VVhats that? Then we are enemies to the Iewes. Come, come, we must needes haue you friendes, & thou'st doe him some good offices. They say the Lord Piso, hath bin a good Clyent to thy elder Ladie of late. And so was I too, Ile be sworne.
speeches.Kni:: Nay, you were a most monstrous puppie. God bewe Signior. Where then? What nation art? O then thou canst make glasses. Why art so melancholie? Fleir, is the gentleman vsher that I preferd to your Ladies in any fauour with them? And how liues he with am. Signeur, I must confesse, I am beholding to your Ladie; and to tell you truly, I haue much affected her since I first saw her. Nay, I haue no reason to thinke the worse of her for the report of the worlde; for the world signeur per chance speakes ill of you, or me. Ile vse thee well. Sure then Fleir she has eaten too much raw fruit. Sure ther. t'is so, I should send her something to comfort her nowe beeing sicke: what doest thinke were best Fleir? Mas, and thou saiest true, Ile goe buy one straight, and yet now I remember me, t'is no great matter if I defer it till she be well, it shall be so Fleir, I will. Yet many of our Ladies delight much in the Scot tish Musicke. Who wee? Weele stabb them. Tis verie deere. The crime is great I must confesse my Lord, but I am sure the proofe can be but little. O had not death arrested me.
T'is a good turne hees no Flie signeur: if a were, a would burne his wings. In what countrie wert borne? Saue you O signeur. I hope shee doth not, Woot dwell with me? And thou with me. O Fleir how does thy Ladie? And how does she? ha, how does she? No, Oates is too great a binder after her Phy sicke, I care not if I goe and visite her, and carrie her a Woodcocke. I, I meane so, but how should I carrie him Fleir? Tush, I keepe a boy for such vses. Yes, to weare a garded Cloke. No, not till I be richly married: hee should weare one now, if my money were come out o'th Countrey. Faith I was knighted to get mee a good wife Fleir. I, but say it should bee proou'd afterwards t'was not true. I would be loath to leaue my truth so far hence. But Fleir is not thy Lady a vertuous Gentlewoman? Of what I prethe? I, I warrant her, O she can endure no bawdrie, shee spits when she heares one speake on't. Shees wondrous musicall too. Be these good tunes Fleir? Thou hast a good wit Fleir: if I were a greatman thou shouldst be my Secretarie. Faith I am going to thy Ladies Fleir. Why sir, I hope I am a Knight, and Knights are be fore Gentlemen. Faith I. Doe, and as occasion serues Ile preferre thee. Assure ye Ladie, your gift of loue to mee shall bee deserued, though nothing but my liues deare breath re quite its. They shall not liue. But where shall we get the poyson? because you knowe t'is daungerous, and will breede suspect where ere wee buy it. What poysons haue you? As how? I doe forgiue you Lady with my soule.
speeches.Pet: Fayth Ladie, would you bestowe but one fauour of me. Vpon any conditions. What are they Fleire?
Why doe you enquire it then?
speeches.Sp:: Looke, looke, this fellow is like your vpright shoo, he will serue either foote. Why, how now signeur, what sayes the Ladie will she loue thee man? Well thanke her for't: And you are sorie for't signeur, are you not? Forgiue him good Ladie, pra'y forgiue him, To this you sweare. Come Signior, you haue kneeld to a faire end, to get you a Mistris, and heere you haue for sworne her. Adew Signior. Who doost serue? What doost want? Whats thy profession? A Courtier! come Gentlemen, I like this fellowe so well that ile prefer him straite. Why a sould his soule to the Deuillman, for the vel uet that lines his cloake. I haue no reason Lady. That with a number oft hath bought. Come Gentlemen will you bee going? How now Fleire? Why are ye enemies? Why didst not strike him agen? Why her Ancient? Because thy Ladies liue like the Beadles of Bride well. By the sinnes of the people. I tell thee I was in hell. As broad as the space between two lines in a Chaun cerie bill. O the diuels are excellent companions, theile drink your Dutch captains, or Court Ladies spunges. Alas for a small fault.
speeches.Pet;: Faith I can get but a colde comfort of her: For what?
speeches.Sp,: Why, for her cold comfort, shee gaue it thee to coole the heate of thy nose man? What? Nay, a deales with him, as a does with his Tailor, goes vpon trust and meanes to pay them both at the latter day. Yes, one of them asked if he were a celestriall or a ter restrial Knight, & he very ignorant lie asked what Knights they were? your terrestriall Knight quoth she, is of a grosse element, and liues vppon landes of his owne, but your ce lestrial Knight, hee liues by the Heire, that is, by his elder Brother. He it was, was Knighted, when so few scapt the sword, and he it is that now liues by the sword. Faith as some Courtiers doe, laugh at that he did not vnderstand, and swore an oath or two of the new fashion, as, by my conscience Ladie you haue a verie good spirit, & so after two or three Court complements, beseech'd the Ladies retaine him still in their good graces, kist his hand and went his way. VVhat's that? O signor, condemne not all for some, indeede I must confesse there haue been Ladies at executions. A forked tree, why what tree doost thou thinke shee would haue made? But Fleire, how does the Gentleman Vsher liue with thy Ladies? How a peny a sheete? Come, a shall goe, for there will bee his Mistresse Madam Fromaga. O I, the Diuels are but our Apes man.
speeches.Ruf;: Why, how now signeur? at blind-man-buffe? bob'd on either side?
speeches.Ruf:: I, come: Ile beginne to her ( tab ) why, what a rogue art thou to offer a faire Ladie an emptie pipe?
speeches.Piso:: Had you no body signeur to haue bob'd with an emptie Pipe but her? Looke you signeur, he told you there was no way to get her good will but by kneeling; for he that will haue a womans loue must stoope. Come Fleir shall we see thy Ladies? Why should I loue her? because shes faire, because shees faire; because shee's a whore: for if she wore not faire, she would not be a whore; & if she were not faire, I should not loue her: Ergo, if shee were not a whore I shoulde not loue her: well concluded witte, well concluded wit; there is no man breathing could loue her but I, shee's a whore, yet her beautie haunts me like a Ghost, I cannot sleepe for't, her remembrance rides me like the Mare a nights, I cannot rest for't, what shall I doe? I shall burst boy. Will thy tongue be secret? What vs? First murther them. Let little children feare the shallow Brookes, for I can swim though't be through Seas of blood; let foolish feare goe dwell with women, for bloodie resolution shall not part from me, Ile kill them both euen with mine owne hands, Ile doo't. Weele fight with them. In which ile mingle mingle such a dram, as they shall ride to heauen in post, vnlesse they misse the way.
speeches.Kni,: Had you no bodie else signeur, to breake an emptie ieast on but this Ladie? Why a Cat hath nine liues sir, and wilt not poyson a woman, seeing twill poyson a Cat?
I faith now thar't a combe for any case. Farwell Signior. Then thou shalt liue with me. Adew. O that I should loue a whore, a very common Co catrise, my thoughts are drown'd in a gulf of sinne, shee's a very Canniball, which doth deuoure mans flesh, and a Horse-leach that sucks out mens best blouds perfection: a very prisoners box, thats ope for euery mans beneuole ̄ ce: and I am Heire vnto a Duke, yet loue her: doth any man heere loue a whore? I, who? I, I, I, tis I, an arrant puncke & common hirde Hackney, and yet I loue her; I adore her, I doate on her, I worshippe her, O would some goodman would cut my throate, and put me out of paine—of paine, O that nature would not make an honest woman! Yes. yes, But Fleire woot helpe me, woot helpe me man? Doe not vex me, doe not torment me: doe not tor ture me vpon the racke of ieastes, I tell thee if shee please, she may turne. Yet againe, now the Deuill take thy body, and dam nation light vpon thy soule, destruction on thy bones, confusion in thy marrow, dost scorne me, mocke me, vexe me, torment mee? dost? dost? Ile hang my selfe, nay, Ile damne my self rather then loue thy Ladie, and be abusd by thee: I will, I will. I graunt it. O that I had the reason of a Sailor to knowe her like a rocke, that I might saile from her and auoide her: or as a vertuous man knowes sinne, to loath and leaue it. And yet shee's wondrous faire, I would she were as honest: kinde v sage may reclaime her from her sinne, and make her stoupe vnto her Husbands will, as doth a wel-mand Hauke vnto the lure. O but her beautie may excuse the folly of her youth, tis want of maintenance hath ouerthrowne her, want and pride are two notorious bawdes: want makes the noblest creature sell her soule for golde, and pride doth make the gallants stoope to lust. And tis well done, let euerie member weare that which it won: why shold the head studdy to maintaine the foote? Why should not euery member like a mechanicke man in a common-wealth, labour in his own trade to main taine it selfe? then since euery thing must liue, I wil no more condemne beautie for being clad in luxurye, but hence foorth I will loue her, and let my passion smoothly swimme along the streame of loues affection: hencefoorth I will no more with foule and hated thoughts, abuse so rare a crea ture, whose behauiour and discourse, inchantes the eares of men, and driues the world into a wonder—ay me! Go go, I will: but O vnhappie fate, When youth and weakenes must support our state. Where's your Maister fellow? But art sure twill poyson a man? Yea? is there good in ill? Thrice Reuerend Iudges, and therefore honored Lords, I must confesse, that like a skilfull dancer, I haue truely footed folly, yet like a learner in my course of life, trod much out of measure, I haue liu'd like an vnbackt colt proud and wanton, my tree of life hath borne more leaues then fruite, I neuer was deboash'd & steard away my daies enen in a sea of sinne. Alas my Lord, this is soone answered, for though that I haue surfeited on sinne, yet haue I not bin drunke with blood. O conscience wonldst thou giue me leaue! Let them call backe the banisht Signior Antifront whome they & we, and al haue wrong'd: O could I liue but to inquire him out, in satisfaction of his wronges, ide marry his eldest Daughter, and whilst a liu'd a should be restored to his estate, but O hee's—
But I am not sir, for I am sicke. Poore. Money. Yes. Fleire. O Signior, you may snuffe out your smoke here Signior, and saue your oath too, heere are no Cuckold ma kers. No, not I; ile not make my nose a red Herring, ile not hang him ith' smoke. What! shall wee embrace? shall we haue red-nos'd Corporals here: what you rogue? will you turne Sumner? away you whale-nosd rogue away, goe, snufle, snufle in the Ocean, away you slaue. Indeede Madam, drinke lightens the head, the heart, the heeles, the pot, the purse; but it makes heauie chamberpots, full bowels, and foule roomes enough. Faith for mine owne part when I had a stomacke, I shoulde like it best in it owne naked kinde, without anie sauce at all. Faith they say your Ladyes cannot endure the old fashion Spurre, they say it hanges to a mans heele like a Wheele-barrow, but they loue the fine little Scottes Spurre, it makes the Court Gennet curuet, curuet gal lantly. If I should tell you, I feare your Ladiships woulde be angrie. I would be loath to displease you. Faith they say your Ladiships are a couple of state ly Curtizans. By my troth they said stately whores. O my good preferrer, how does your worshippe, you are a stranger heere. O my Lord, you are a welcome man. I, I, I, Come: but my good Lord youle bee a wel come man, for I haue heard her often sweare, that had she such a Husband, a man so richly deckt in vertuous orna ments, shee woulde forsake this life, her-selfe, nay, her verie being, to be your's; O my good Lord, shee loues you deerly. Why my good Lord? But say she may turne my Lord. O my Lord, penitence doth purge a spotted soule, and better leaue sinne late then not at all: and I doe knowe my Lorde, that for your loue from her immodest life sheel turne. Great, great: a kisses his hand with an excellent grace, and a will leire and fleire vppon am, hee's partly their Phisitian, a makes am Suppositories, and giues am Glisters. No, no, no. I, I, hoe, whose within there? Whither are you going? Come, come ▪ Ile preferre you both, thou shalt serue a Countrey-man of mine, hees going to trauaile: shalt goe with him, & thou shalt serue one of my Ladies. Then let them march both hand in hand in one way. O God, I think the path to hell that women tread is broder then the way men goe: how they walke by cou ples to the Deuill? I deliuerd your letter sir, and she thanks you for't: Faith not well, she has taken phisick, and your gen tleman vsher there ministers to her: shees very great, and she sayes she feeles much stirring in her bellie. Send her an Oten cake, t'is a good Northern token: sir Raph Shaue sent his Mistris one, but I think a meant to ride a iourney on her, and thought Otes woulde make her trauell well. You'le goe alone sir. For nothing else? I wonder you would be knighted sir, since your mo ney is so long a comming, that you cannot maintaine your knighthood gallantly. Get you a good wife? Why looke you sir, speake but the Golden tongue verie perfectly, marry you must speake it well, and call some great Lorde cousen: t'will get you a better wife then three hundred pound ioynter. You may report you haue Colepits too,, t'is a warme commoditie I can tell you: they may bee sent about by water; if they nere come, as your money dooth not, you maye curse the windes, or complaine of Ship wracke: and then though't bee a lie t'is drown'd. True? Gods my life, shee's a wise woman that will goe as far as new Castle to search the depth of a Cole-pit for your truth. But I am sure heele bring his honestie no nearer hi ther; but that comes about by water too as his mony does. O yes sir, I often find her in deepe contemplation. I, with their Instruments. And I hope I should discharge the place suffici ently: for I haue learning enough to take a bribe, and witte enough to be prowd: but whither are you going now sir? You will not speake with am now; for my Ladies will speake with none but Gentlemen. What Knights before Gentlemen, say ye? Thats strange, they were wont to bee Gentlemen fore they were knighted: but for this newes Ile folow you. To her agen man, doe not leaue her, the Moone is now vpon change, she will turne. But beleeue me my little Gallants, yee play the Boyes well. Saue you Signior. I am a Florentine borne. I shall remember still not to forget what you giue me in charge. I would be loath to be found otherwise. Now come away my Customers, I hope I am fitted for an Apothecary ▪ s'hart I thinke ime turnd coniurer, for I haue no sooner cal'd ▪ but the Deuils are appeared, what do yee lacke Gentlemen? My Maister is gone into Italie sir, but if you want any thing, ile vse you well, if you want any drugs to make Lotiums, any Restringent Powders, anie Aqua Mirabilis, any Cordiall receipts, or anie Pretious poysons? Excellent good sir, as euer was tasted, looke you sir, this poysons by the smell, this by the sight, and this by the tastes. Am I sure on't? why tak't vpon my credit, twil poi son any vermine, except it be a woman, for twill poyson a Cat sir. O sir tis verie cheape, considering the goodnesse on't. I pray sir your name. Come, come, thou didst but dreame thou wert in hell. And how long was't ere thou camest thither? O sir, there's the conscience on't, say the Plaintiffe be in one line, and the defendant in an other, they being ene mies, wer't either conscience or honestie in the Clearke to thrust them no neare togither, that they might goe to gither by th'eares? but yfaith what good fellowship was there in hell? Why are there a companie of Porters in hell? And good reason, why coulde not shee haue kept her Trade, and beene a Puritane, as well as a Puritane keepe her Religion, and yet bee of her Trade? Why was he damn'd? I prethe what wast? Were there no Lawyers in hell? speeches.Fro:: A foule Ladie? y'are a sawcy Iacke to call mee so, that you are.
Kindenes; faith sir you are mistaken in mee, you must seeke your flurts some other where, and I pra'y come not to make a foole of me: alas man though I am a waiting woman ▪ do not think I spend my time in nothing but tem pering of colours, working of drawn-worke, warming of Smockes, and pinning in of ruffes, faith yes.
speeches.From,: Faith I, and ye come to begin your knauerie on me, ile take you down: I am none of your young simpering waiting-women, that are asham'd to be counted proud, & therefore suffer euerie Seruingman to vse them at their pleasure.
speeches.Piso: Vntoucht? weele doo't. But for the meanes.
speeches.Na: I wonder thoult liue in such a sinfull place.
speeches.Na,: But what shall we doe in this matter?
speeches.Both:: Doe it and we shall euer thanke thee. Come lets about it then. Tis too true my Lord.
Whats this? O this is Arringus; this makes the old man able, and the young man lustie, strengthneth the nerues & doth concoct the bloud, and her name is written on the box, because my wife should knowe it in my ab sence: this is Ciuet, this comes from the Cats taile, I would my were such a Cat: this perfumes your Ladies, and not without cause, for some, I meane whose sweet breath is dead, and teeth mourne in blacke for the losse on't this makes your young Gallants smell them nine daies before they see them, like young poops: this drug is pretious & deere; whats this? O this is the sptrit of roses, nineteene bushels and a halfe of Roses make but an ounce, & a dram on't, tis made of the Quinressence of the water after the fifteenth distillation: none may kisse a Ladie after shee hath annointed her lips with this, vnder the degree of a Lord at least, tis worth nine poundes an ounce, yet I could neuer still it so.
speeches.Alu:: Y`are welcome sir, what doe ye lacke? What countrie man art thou? Well Iacomo, if I finde thee honest thou shalt find me liberall. Continue so, I prethee, and so farwell Iaques, but ile enforme my wife before I goe to respect thee according to thy merrit.
speeches.Alu,: Thou art my Countrie man, and therefore welcom and in happie time, for I am bound for Italy, and want a man to take charge of my Shop, onely this is all: I shall re quire of you, bee carefull of your cares, and obedient to your Mistresse.
speeches.Pet ▪: Not I, I was not bid.
I am a poore Gentleman, whose fortunes much de pend vpon his fauours, and indeede sir I am his Clarke. Indeede sir hee's not well, but if you please to send by me the substance of your busines I shall very carefullie deliuer it.
speeches.Mitti:: Sir I shall deliuer your message, and will returne his answere to you presently.
speeches.Ser:: Sir my maister hath receiued your message, & hath sent this Ring as a token to Doctor Caius, desiring him, since my maisters health will not permit him to be present, to proceede alone to iudgement, and so commends his loue to him.
speeches.Spar:: For hauing alwayes money in his purse.
VVil't please yee haue the prisoners brought foorth?
VVee can doe nothing till wee heare from Doctor Ferrio, to knowe his pleasure in these procee dings. Sir, wee knowe the ring and you are verie wel come, and so I pra'y assume his place. My Lord, you are heere indited of a hatefull crime, & I am verie sorry to see you in this sort stand here.
Was any man sent to him?
speeches.Caius,: Yes, Fleire, the Lady Floridaes man, which is not yet returned. Intreate him to come in. I, both of them. And in, that sea my Lord, you bore so great a saile as you haue ouer set your barke of life, and heere you are accused my Lord, euen of a hatefull crime, so is the Knight there for poisoning two Gentlemen, Sparke and Ruffell, how doe you answere this my Lord?
speeches.Iaylor,: Reuerend Iudges: heere's a Doctor at doore de sires admittance. Is it your pleasure the Prisoners be brought footh.
speeches.Cai:: Ladies you know moste, and therefore tis fittest most you speake. Reuerend Iudges, God wil by some meanes punish euerie sinne, and though against my will, yet by my consci ence I am enforced to vnmaske my Ladies vilianies, the murther for which the Lord and Knight are like to die, was first plotted by them: the two Pages with my selfe did heare it: the Prisoners in this action, are inforc't by Sacra ment to be secret, and thus intreating heauen in Iustice, still to ayde you. speeches.Fal:: And wee no doubt my Lordes, had long ere this breath'd out our liues like them, but that we had the lesser quantisie, for being esteemed the weaker vessels, they thought the lesser blow would breake vs.
speeches.Fle: Why then vppon this hand I heare arrest you both, vpon your liues.
speeches.2, Iudg,: They are sworne not to reueale it,
speeches.Both,: Heere my Lord. The letter speakes nothing but the truth.
Long liue my honored Lord and mighty Duke of Florence.
speeches.Mes,: My honored Lord, your Father is deceased, and the state of Florence by me hath sent their Letters and al legiance.
